name: Seagrass meadows
lead: An underwater meadow. A powerful carbon store.
description: Seagrasses are flowering plants, not seaweed. Their leaves take up carbon through photosynthesis, while roots and rhizomes slow water and help trap organic matter in the seabed.
landmark: A 2022 study mapped an estimated 66,000–92,000 km² of seagrass on the Bahamas Banks: an exceptionally large seagrass ecosystem.
carbon: Organic matter buried in low-oxygen sediment can remain stored long after a leaf dies. Protecting the seabed matters as much as protecting the plants.
threat: Dredging, poor water quality and marine heatwaves can reduce light, damage plants and disturb carbon-rich sediment.
action: Protect water quality, prevent anchor damage and restore meadows in suitable, well-monitored sites.

layer.title: Global Distribution of Seagrasses
layer.detail: Published point and polygon records from field surveys, literature and remote sensing. Mapped presence is not a complete census; blank areas can be unobserved.

name: Mangrove forests
description: Mangroves grow along sheltered tropical and subtropical coasts. Their roots hold sediment, provide habitat and slow moving water, while wood and soils retain organic carbon.
landmark: The Sundarbans is the world’s largest contiguous mangrove forest, spanning the delta between Bangladesh and India.
carbon: Carbon is held in living biomass, roots and deep coastal soils. Conversion and drainage can expose that stored carbon to decomposition.
threat: Coastal conversion, altered freshwater flows and sea-level rise can interrupt sediment supply and squeeze forests against developed land.
action: Keep tidal connections open and protect existing forests before attempting new planting.

layer.title: Global Mangrove Watch
layer.detail: The 2020 mangrove extent layer combines radar and optical earth observation. Historical service layers are not drawn on top of 2020.

name: Tidal salt marshes
lead: Carbon storage, renewed with every tide.
description: Salt-tolerant grasses occupy the space between land and sea. Tides carry fine sediment into these wetlands, and dense root systems help build organic-rich soils.
landmark: The southeastern US coast hosts extensive tidal marsh landscapes. Hilton Head is a representative site, rather than a claim to the world’s largest single marsh.
carbon: Sediment accretion and slow decomposition can retain organic carbon. The long-term balance also depends on erosion, methane and changes to tidal exchange.
threat: Development and rising seas can trap marshes against hard shorelines. Drainage removes the wet conditions that protect stored carbon.
action: Restore tidal exchange and leave room for marshes to migrate inland.
photoFile: Salt Marsh at Fish Haul Creek, Hilton Head Island.jpg
photoPlace: Fish Haul Creek · Hilton Head Island
sourceTitle: McOwen et al. · A global map of saltmarshes · 2017

layer.title: Global Distribution of Saltmarshes
layer.detail: A global compilation of mapped saltmarsh polygons and occurrence points. Coverage and survey dates vary by country.

name: Tropical forests
lead: A forest that moves carbon, water and life.
description: Tropical trees absorb carbon as they grow and hold it in wood, roots and soils. The Amazon is Earth’s largest tropical rainforest and an essential part of the global carbon cycle.
landmark: The Amazon spans multiple South American countries. This pin near Manaus represents the wider forest, not a mapped boundary.
carbon: Photosynthesis stores carbon in plant tissues, while respiration, decomposition and fire return it. Whether a region is a net sink varies across space and time.
threat: Deforestation, fragmentation, drought and fire can turn long-standing carbon stores into sources of emissions.
action: Avoid deforestation, reconnect habitat and support durable, locally led forest protection.
photoPlace: Amazon forest · north of Manaus, Brazil

layer.title: Tropical tree cover
layer.detail: Tree-cover class highlighted within 23.44° north/south. Includes plantations and other tree cover: it is not a map of intact rainforest. WMS is a visualization service, not an area-measurement product.

name: Kelp forests
description: Kelp are large brown algae that grow along cool, rocky coasts. They support marine food webs and take up dissolved carbon as they build new tissue.
landmark: Australia’s Great Southern Reef is a continent-scale temperate reef system with extensive kelp habitats. This is a representative kelp location, not a surveyed polygon.
carbon: Detached kelp can be carried away and some carbon may reach deep water or sediment. Fast growth alone does not establish how much carbon stays stored, or for how long.
threat: Marine heatwaves and changes in grazing can shift kelp forests to bare or turf-covered reefs.
action: Reduce climate pressure, improve coastal water quality and use site-specific restoration informed by local ecology.

layer.title: Modelled global kelp biome
layer.detail: A published model of the global kelp biome. It represents modelled habitat suitability, not a live satellite inventory or proof of kelp in each location.

name: Phytoplankton
description: Phytoplankton use sunlight and dissolved carbon to grow near the ocean surface. They feed marine food webs, and a fraction of organic matter sinks into deeper water.
landmark: Patagonian Shelf blooms can stretch over huge areas of the South Atlantic. Their extent changes with seasons, currents and nutrient supply.
carbon: The biological pump moves some organic carbon away from the surface. Chlorophyll reveals a pigment associated with phytoplankton, not a direct measurement of permanent carbon removal.
threat: Warming and altered circulation change nutrient supply and bloom timing. Responses differ among ocean regions and species.
action: Reduce nutrient pollution and support ocean observation and climate protection.

layer.title: Surface chlorophyll-a
layer.detail: Near-surface chlorophyll-a in mg/m³. Clouds and missing overpasses create gaps. Pigment concentration is not a species census or carbon credit estimate. The multi-colour badge identifies the continuous layer; use the publisher legend for numerical interpretation.

name: Coral reefs
lead: A living city, built from carbonate.
description: Reef-building corals host photosynthetic partners and construct calcium-carbonate skeletons. Their reefs support extraordinary biodiversity and protect coastlines.
landmark: The Great Barrier Reef is the world’s largest coral reef ecosystem. This pin represents the system, not its full geographic boundary.
carbon: Coral carbonate is different from buried organic carbon. Calcification can release CO₂; a reef’s climate balance cannot be inferred by counting its skeletons.
threat: Ocean warming drives bleaching, while acidification affects carbonate chemistry. Pollution and physical disturbance add local pressure.
action: Cut warming, protect water quality and safeguard connected reef habitats.
duration: Not equivalent to a CO₂ sink
sourceTitle: UNESCO World Heritage · Great Barrier Reef

layer.title: Global warm-water coral reefs
layer.detail: Mapped warm-water reef points and polygons. This is habitat extent, not live coral condition, bleaching severity or cold-water coral coverage.
